A Safe Action Is Not Enough: Feasible-Future Decoding for Vision-Language-Action Policies

Tu Nguyen1, Matthieu Zimmer2 Vu Anh Vu1 Ziyi Wang1,3 Jannik Hammel Nielsen1 Xuebing Zhou1 Haitham Bou Ammar2,4 1Huawei Heisenberg Research Center  2Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab 3TU Berlin  4UCL Center for AI ††thanks: Corresponding author: tu.nguyen@huawei.com
Abstract

A safe action is not necessarily a viable one. Under a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy, an action can be likely and locally admissible yet leave no policy-supported route to safe task completion. We call this the feasibility–likelihood gap: likelihood ranks the current action, whereas feasibility depends on the futures that remain after it.

We derive the exact next-block marginal of the history-conditioned policy–environment trajectory law restricted to safe task completion. The derivation exposes a candidate-dependent feasible-future mass with two roles: its support records whether safe completion remains possible under the frozen continuation process, and its magnitude measures how much weighted safe-completion mass is preserved. Exact evaluation is impractical online, so we develop a selective finite-candidate approximation, derive conditions for recovering the best retained viable candidate, and instantiate it as an alarm-triggered, training-free reranker.

On Safety-CHORES, VICS-G lowers mean cumulative safety cost by 1.9%1.9\%–57.5%57.5\% across six settings while remaining within 2.52.5 percentage points of policy sampling in success and 0.820.82 steps in mean episode length. The resulting decoder is tied to an exact policy-relative safe-completion target, yet requires neither retraining of the base policy nor online trajectory rollouts.

1 Introduction

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map visual observations and natural-language instructions into robot actions, drawing on broad semantic and motor priors learned from large-scale vision–language pretraining and robot demonstrations. Systems such as RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023), PaLM-E (Driess et al., 2023), OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024), Octo (Octo Model Team et al., 2024), and π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2024) illustrate this breadth. Given an observation oto_{t}, instruction xx, and interaction history hth_{t}, the policy defines

at:t+H−1∼πθ(⋅∣ot,x,ht).a_{t:t+H-1}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid o_{t},x,h_{t}).

This distribution captures intent, affordances, and embodiment regularities. It ranks the policy’s next move; safe completion depends on where that move can lead.

An action can look safe in the moment and still steer the agent into a dead end. A candidate may be likely and pass every local safety check, yet leave no route to safe task completion under the frozen policy. We call this the feasibility–likelihood gap. Figure 1 makes the practical motivation concrete: reducing cost must be assessed alongside the ability to continue and complete the task. Deployment-time constrained decoding provides a natural way to address this gap by revising action selection as execution unfolds, without changing the underlying policy (Zhang et al., 2025; Kapoor et al., 2025; Hsu et al., 2023).

Looking beyond the next action is especially difficult in robotics. In autoregressive language generation, a fixed prefix and candidate token determine the next symbolic prefix exactly, so future continuations branch from a fully determined prefix (Ji et al., 2025). Robot actions instead induce physical transitions,

st+H∼P(⋅∣st,at:t+H−1),s_{t+H}\sim P(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t:t+H-1}),

and the same observable history and action block can lead to different successor states. Partial observability and execution uncertainty can alter reachability, visibility, and collision geometry, changing which safe continuations remain available. A principled safe-completion target must therefore account for both future policy choices and environment dynamics.

We derive the target from the joint policy–environment trajectory law. Weighting trajectories by reward and cost, restricting them to safe task completion, and marginalizing over the future suffix yields an exact next-block marginal. This marginal combines the action prior and local reward–cost terms with the weighted mass of safe, successful continuations—the feasible-future mass.

This quantity is policy-relative by construction. A zero mass does not mean that safe completion is physically impossible; another controller may still succeed. Rather, it means that the frozen policy–environment process places no probability on safe completion after that action. The mass therefore captures two complementary aspects of the future: whether safe completion remains within the policy’s support and, when it does, how much weighted continuation mass is preserved. We formalize these as support and magnitude.

Computing this quantity exactly is generally impractical at decision time, so we turn to a selective finite-candidate approximation. Its score combines policy likelihood, local robustness, and a bounded continuation term, while a gate decides whether the sampled action is worth revisiting at all. Only then does the decoder rerank a small candidate set. This saves computation, but a dead end accepted by the gate never reaches the reranker. We therefore analyze intervention loss alongside errors in candidate availability, support handling, and approximate scoring. The resulting conditions show when the best retained viable candidate can still be recovered without reconstructing the exact mass.

We instantiate the rollout-free approximation as a training-free reranker driven by the current observation and interaction history. Across six Safety-CHORES settings (Zhang et al., 2025), the generic VICS-G configuration consistently lowers observed safety cost while retaining near-policy task completion and episode length. This combination is the central practical benefit: a frozen VLA can act more safely while sustaining progress toward its task. Evaluating safety jointly with completion and episode length (Fan et al., 2026) makes this benefit visible and distinguishes it from cost reductions that accompany early termination.

The same perspective extends naturally to imperfect execution and explicit lookahead. On safety-aligned Fetch, execution feedback yields a favorable observed safety–completion trade-off under perturbed actions, while a matched ablation supports preservation of task success within the preset tolerance. The theory invites us to test rollouts, letting sampled futures shape the next action. Even in simulation, however, those futures are costly to generate and only as reliable as the dynamics model behind them. We therefore study VICS-R, a modest rollout augmentation of VICS-G guided by safe-completion estimates under a limited simulation budget. On Fetch, it improves observed safe success and further reduces cost (Section 4.4). These studies connect a rollout-free deployment-time decoder to richer sources of execution and continuation evidence.

Our contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    An exact next-block target for policy-relative safe completion. We derive the next-action marginal of a prior-preserving trajectory law restricted to safe completion. Feasible-future mass connects the current action to the safe continuations it leaves open: support captures whether such continuations remain, while magnitude captures their weighted mass.

  2. 2.

    A selective approximation theory with explicit failure interfaces. We separate intervention, coverage, support, and ranking errors, derive a recovery margin for the best retained viable action, and show when finite continuation rollouts preserve the ideal winner.

  3. 3.

    A practical route to safer execution with frozen policies. VICS-G combines selective, training-free intervention with consistent observed cost reductions and near-policy task completion across six Safety-CHORES settings. Ablations of execution feedback and rollout augmentation test the value of evidence from realized actions and sampled continuations.

2 Local Safety and Policy-Supported Viability

We consider a frozen policy πθ\pi_{\theta} over HH-action blocks a≡at:t+H−1a\equiv a_{t:t+H-1}, conditioned on the observable history ℋt=(ot,x,ht)\mathcal{H}_{t}=(o_{t},x,h_{t}). Executing a block changes the latent state according to st+H∼P(⋅∣st,a)s_{t+H}\sim P(\cdot\mid s_{t},a). Together with the transition kernel PP and observation process Ω\Omega, the policy induces a history-conditioned law p0​(τ∣ℋt)p_{0}(\tau\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}) over future trajectories. Let 𝒢x\mathcal{G}_{x} denote those trajectories that complete xx while satisfying the designated hard safety budget.

At inference time, the decoder receives a finite policy-supported candidate set 𝒜K={a1,…,aNt}\mathcal{A}_{K}=\{a^{1},\ldots,a^{N_{t}}\} and returns one of its members. Here KK denotes the proposal budget; retaining the policy sample alongside top-KK actions gives Nt=|𝒜K|≤K+1N_{t}=|\mathcal{A}_{K}|\leq K+1.

A local robustness decoder combines the policy’s preference with the predicted safety margin of the next block:

Sloc(a)=logπθ(a∣ℋt)+λcρC(τ^t:t+H),S_{\mathrm{loc}}(a)=\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})+\lambda_{c}\rho_{C}(\widehat{\tau}_{t:t+H}), (1)

where τ^t:t+H\widehat{\tau}_{t:t+H} is the predicted local trace, λc≥0\lambda_{c}\geq 0 weights local robustness, and larger ρC\rho_{C} indicates greater predicted constraint margin. Likelihood expresses what the policy favors; local robustness assesses the predicted next block. Neither alone tells us whether the action leaves a supported route to safe completion.

Definition 1 (Feasibility–likelihood gap).

A feasibility–likelihood gap occurs at ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} if there exist a,b∈𝒜Ka,b\in\mathcal{A}_{K} such that

log⁡πθ​(a∣ℋt)>log⁡πθ​(b∣ℋt),\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})>\log\pi_{\theta}(b\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}),

but

ℙp0[τ∈𝒢x∣ℋt,a]<ℙp0[τ∈𝒢x∣ℋt,b].\mathbb{P}_{p_{0}}[\tau\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},a]<\mathbb{P}_{p_{0}}[\tau\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},b].

Each probability measures safe task completion after choosing the candidate, averaging over latent-state uncertainty, environment outcomes, and subsequent actions of the frozen policy. The policy favors aa, yet its own continuation process gives bb a higher probability of safe completion.

Two failure modes make this gap concrete. An unsafe shortcut violates a local constraint. A safe dead end passes the local check but leaves zero probability of safe completion under the frozen continuation process. A dead end for this policy may still allow safe task completion under another controller. The question is how the safe futures each action leaves open should shape the choice made now.

3 From Trajectories to Feasible Futures

We now derive how the safe, task-completing futures an action leaves open shape its score. The reference construction follows standard KL-regularized control and control-as-inference machinery (Todorov, 2006; Toussaint, 2009; Levine, 2018). We first derive the ideal next-action score, then show where selective decoding over a finite candidate set can depart from it. Appendix B.1 gives the variational formulation and regularity conditions, while Appendix E verifies the principal identities by exact finite-model enumeration.

3.1 A feasible-future identity

The prior-preserving safe-completion reference law is

q⋆(τ∣ℋt)=1Z⁡(ℋt)p0(τ∣ℋt)𝟏{τ∈𝒢x}exp(βRx(τ)−λC(τ)),q^{\star}(\tau\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})=\frac{1}{Z(\mathcal{H}_{t})}p_{0}(\tau\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\mathbf{1}\{\tau\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\}\exp\!\left(\beta R_{x}(\tau)-\lambda C(\tau)\right), (2)

provided 0<Z⁡(ℋt)<∞0<Z(\mathcal{H}_{t})<\infty. The indicator restricts the reference law to safe task completion; the exponential weight expresses reward–cost preferences among those trajectories. This is a reference distribution, not a claim that the deployed decoder solves a global control problem.

Write a future realization as (a,ξ)(a,\xi), where a≡at:t+H−1a\equiv a_{t:t+H-1} is the candidate command block. The residual suffix ξ\xi includes stochastic execution of aa and subsequent latent states, observations, policy actions, and outcomes. Suffix reward and cost notation suppresses conditioning on (ℋt,a)(\mathcal{H}_{t},a). Only history-and-action-measurable terms enter Rloc,ClocR_{\mathrm{loc}},C_{\mathrm{loc}} and are pulled outside the expectation; random block rewards and collision costs remain inside the continuation expectation.

Theorem 1 (Feasible futures in the blockwise marginal).

Assume

p0​(a,ξ∣ℋt)=πθ​(a∣ℋt)​p0​(ξ∣ℋt,a),p_{0}(a,\xi\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})=\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\,p_{0}(\xi\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},a), (3)

and let reward and cost decompose as

Rx​(a,ξ)\displaystyle R_{x}(a,\xi) =Rloc​(ℋt,a)+Rsuf​(ξ,x),\displaystyle=R_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)+R_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi,x), (4)
C⁡(a,ξ)\displaystyle C(a,\xi) =Cloc​(ℋt,a)+Csuf​(ξ).\displaystyle=C_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)+C_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi). (5)

For cumulative constraints, the remaining budget is included in ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}; Appendix B gives the augmented-state form. Then the next-block marginal of Equation 2 is

q⋆​(a∣ℋt)∝πθ​(a∣ℋt)​exp⁡(β​Rloc​(ℋt,a)−λ​Cloc​(ℋt,a))​Zfeas​(ℋt,a),q^{\star}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\propto\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\exp\!\left(\beta R_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)-\lambda C_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)\right)Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a), (6)

where

Zfeas(ℋt,a)=𝔼ξ∼p0(⋅∣ℋt,a)[𝟏{(a,ξ)∈𝒢x}exp(βRsuf(ξ,x)−λCsuf(ξ))].Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim p_{0}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},a)}\left[\mathbf{1}\{(a,\xi)\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\}\exp\!\left(\beta R_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi,x)-\lambda C_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi)\right)\right]. (7)

Interpretation.

The next-block marginal contains three terms: the frozen action prior, the local reward–cost contribution, and the future preserved by the action. The last term integrates latent-state uncertainty, stochastic execution, future observations, and future policy actions under the frozen continuation process. When β=λ=0\beta=\lambda=0, this factor is simply the conditional probability of safe task completion after the candidate. In particular, Zfeas​(ℋt,a)=0Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=0 means that this process assigns no mass to safe task completion after aa; it does not mean that every controller would fail from the resulting state. Taking the logarithm of the unnormalized marginal gives the ideal score defined later in Equation 13.

Support and magnitude.

Safe completion can remain possible even when the policy is unlikely to find its way there. We therefore separate two questions: does safe completion have positive probability under the frozen continuation process, and, when it does, how much weighted continuation mass remains? Define

χfeas⋆(ℋt,a)=𝟏{Zfeas(ℋt,a)>0},Z¯feas⋆(ℋt,a)={Zfeas​(ℋt,a),Zfeas​(ℋt,a)>0,1,Zfeas​(ℋt,a)=0,\chi_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=\mathbf{1}\{Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)>0\},\qquad\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=\begin{cases}Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a),&Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)>0,\\ 1,&Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=0,\end{cases} (8)

so that

Zfeas​(ℋt,a)=χfeas⋆​(ℋt,a)​Z¯feas⋆​(ℋt,a).Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=\chi_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)\,\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a). (9)

The value 11 off support is a neutral convention. Support is categorical; magnitude is positive and graded on the support. A finite score can make a suspected dead end unlikely, but it cannot reproduce the literal zero, or the −∞-\infty log score, of an action outside the ideal support.

Safe dead ends.

Two candidates can have equal likelihood and identical local reward–cost terms while one has positive feasible-future mass and the other has none. Every local-only score is then indifferent, whereas the ideal blockwise rule assigns the dead end zero mass. Appendix C.4 states this separation formally.

An exact finite witness.

Figure 2 follows four candidates: an unsafe shortcut aUa_{U}, a locally admissible dead end aDa_{D}, and feasible actions aL,aHa_{L},a_{H} with lower and higher continuation magnitude. Each factor changes the winner; Appendix E gives the exact construction.

The witness also exposes the role of intervention: a selective decoder that accepts aDa_{D} at its initial gate never reaches this future-aware comparison.

3.2 Selective finite candidates: four approximation interfaces

The ideal score tells us what to prefer; in practice, however, the decoder sees only a few candidates and an imperfect picture of their futures. We therefore track four approximation interfaces: intervention, whether authorized reranking determines the executed action; coverage, which viable alternatives survive proposal and admission; support, whether viable actions are rejected or dead ends remain eligible; and ranking, how accurately the score orders viable survivors. We first analyze recovery within the reranking branch, then account for retention of the policy sample.

Let apol∈𝒜Ka_{\mathrm{pol}}\in\mathcal{A}_{K} be the policy sample and a0a_{0} the highest-likelihood candidate; they need not coincide. On intervention, the admitted set combines a likelihood trust region with shared safety and task-feasibility checks:

ℬt=𝒜K∩𝒯τ​(a0)∩𝒮pred∩ℱpred.\mathcal{B}_{t}=\mathcal{A}_{K}\cap\mathcal{T}_{\tau}(a_{0})\cap\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{pred}}\cap\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pred}}. (10)

Here 𝒯τ​(a0)\mathcal{T}_{\tau}(a_{0}) limits the policy log-probability gap from a0a_{0}, and 𝒮pred,ℱpred\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{pred}},\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pred}} are predicted-safety and task-feasibility filters (Appendix F). These checks do not determine the true viable set.

The true policy-relative viable subset of ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} is

ℱt={a∈ℬt:Zfeas​(ℋt,a)>0}.\mathcal{F}_{t}=\{a\in\mathcal{B}_{t}:\ Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)>0\}. (11)

Let 𝒟t⊆ℬt\mathcal{D}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{B}_{t} be the candidates rejected by a practical support rule using its available pre-action information. This set need not equal the true dead-end set ℬt∖ℱt={a∈ℬt:Zfeas​(ℋt,a)=0}\mathcal{B}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{t}=\{a\in\mathcal{B}_{t}:Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=0\}. Define

ℱ^t=ℬt∖𝒟t,𝒢t=ℱt∩ℱ^t,ℛt=ℱ^t∖ℱt.\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{t}=\mathcal{B}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{t},\qquad\mathcal{G}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{t}\cap\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{t},\qquad\mathcal{R}_{t}=\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{t}. (12)

Thus ℱ^t\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{t} is the set available for reranking: 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} contains its viable members, and ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} contains its remaining dead ends. The decoder constructs ℱ^t\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{t} from pre-action rules; the split into 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} and ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} is used only for analysis. We do not assume that the decoder knows which surviving candidates truly support safe completion.

Taking the logarithm of the unnormalized marginal in Theorem 1, define the extended-real ideal score

S⋆​(a)=log⁡πθ​(a∣ℋt)+β​Rloc​(ℋt,a)−λ​Cloc​(ℋt,a)+log⁡Zfeas​(ℋt,a),S^{\star}(a)=\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})+\beta R_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)-\lambda C_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)+\log Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a), (13)

with log⁡0=−∞\log 0=-\infty. Maximizing S⋆S^{\star} therefore gives the exact next-block MAP rule induced by Theorem 1. Let S^​(a)\widehat{S}(a) be any finite practical score on ℱ^t\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{t}. Whenever 𝒢t≠∅\mathcal{G}_{t}\neq\emptyset, define the practical support-separation margin

Δtsup=maxg∈𝒢t⁡S^​(g)−maxr∈ℛt⁡S^​(r).\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{sup}}=\max_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}\widehat{S}(g)-\max_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}\widehat{S}(r). (14)

The second maximum is −∞-\infty when ℛt=∅\mathcal{R}_{t}=\emptyset. Thus Δtsup>0\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{sup}}>0 ensures that a retained viable action outranks every remaining dead end. Rejection of viable actions is accounted for separately by the loss Γtrej\Gamma^{\mathrm{rej}}_{t} below.

The next theorem bounds the loss relative to the best retained viable candidate and identifies when that candidate is recovered exactly. Only score differences determine the ranking, so a candidate-independent offset does not affect the recovery guarantee.

Theorem 2 (Selective finite-candidate recovery under partial support).

Let 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} be a finite policy-supported viable comparison set containing ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and, whenever apola_{\mathrm{pol}} is viable, the retained policy sample apola_{\mathrm{pol}}. Because all decision sets are finite, the maxima below are attained. Assume 𝒢t≠∅\mathcal{G}_{t}\neq\emptyset, Δtsup>0\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{sup}}>0, and

|(S^​(a)−S^​(b))−(S⋆​(a)−S⋆​(b))|≤ε∀a,b∈𝒢t.\left|\bigl(\widehat{S}(a)-\widehat{S}(b)\bigr)-\bigl(S^{\star}(a)-S^{\star}(b)\bigr)\right|\leq\varepsilon\qquad\forall a,b\in\mathcal{G}_{t}. (15)

a^=arg​maxa∈ℱ^t⁡S^​(a),a𝒢⋆=arg​maxa∈𝒢t⁡S⋆​(a),aℱ⋆=arg​maxa∈ℱt⁡S⋆​(a),a𝒱⋆=arg​maxa∈𝒱t⁡S⋆​(a),\widehat{a}=\argmax_{a\in\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{t}}\widehat{S}(a),\quad a_{\mathcal{G}}^{\star}=\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}S^{\star}(a),\quad a_{\mathcal{F}}^{\star}=\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{F}_{t}}S^{\star}(a),\quad a_{\mathcal{V}}^{\star}=\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{V}_{t}}S^{\star}(a),

under a common deterministic tie rule. Then a^∈𝒢t\widehat{a}\in\mathcal{G}_{t} and

S⋆​(a𝒢⋆)−S⋆​(a^)≤ε.S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{G}}^{\star})-S^{\star}(\widehat{a})\leq\varepsilon. (16)

If the ideal margin of a𝒢⋆a_{\mathcal{G}}^{\star} over the second-best action in 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} exceeds ε\varepsilon, then a^=a𝒢⋆\widehat{a}=a_{\mathcal{G}}^{\star}; take the margin as +∞+\infty when 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} is a singleton. Moreover,

S⋆​(a𝒱⋆)−S⋆​(a^)≤S⋆​(a𝒱⋆)−S⋆​(aℱ⋆)⏟Γtcov​(proposal/admission coverage)+S⋆​(aℱ⋆)−S⋆​(a𝒢⋆)⏟Γtrej​(false rejection)+ε.S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{V}}^{\star})-S^{\star}(\widehat{a})\leq\underbrace{S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{V}}^{\star})-S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{F}}^{\star})}_{\Gamma^{\mathrm{cov}}_{t}\ \text{(proposal/admission coverage)}}+\underbrace{S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{F}}^{\star})-S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{G}}^{\star})}_{\Gamma^{\mathrm{rej}}_{t}\ \text{(false rejection)}}+\varepsilon. (17)

The three reference actions make the decomposition concrete: a𝒱⋆a_{\mathcal{V}}^{\star} is best in the viable comparison set, aℱ⋆a_{\mathcal{F}}^{\star} is best after proposal and admission, and a𝒢⋆a_{\mathcal{G}}^{\star} is best after support rejection. The nested sets 𝒢t⊆ℱt⊆𝒱t\mathcal{G}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{t} make the first two losses nonnegative: they measure opportunities lost before ranking begins. The remaining ranking loss within 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} is bounded by ε\varepsilon.

The bound concerns the ideal action score at the current history. Support separation, Δtsup>0\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{sup}}>0, ensures that the practical winner is viable even when some dead ends remain eligible. The gate and final authorization separately determine whether that winner is executed.

Selective intervention.

For VICS-G, let gt∈{0,1}g_{t}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether the initial gate invokes reranking. Set jt=1j_{t}=1 exactly when gt=1g_{t}=1, the surviving set is nonempty, and final replacement authorization accepts a^\widehat{a}; otherwise set jt=0j_{t}=0. The deployed action is

atdep={a^,jt=1,apol,jt=0.a_{t}^{\mathrm{dep}}=\begin{cases}\widehat{a},&j_{t}=1,\\ a_{\mathrm{pol}},&j_{t}=0.\end{cases} (18)

For nonempty 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t}, define ℒtdep=S⋆​(a𝒱⋆)−S⋆​(atdep)\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{dep}}=S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{V}}^{\star})-S^{\star}(a_{t}^{\mathrm{dep}}) and

Γtgate=S⋆​(a𝒱⋆)−S⋆​(apol)∈[0,∞].\Gamma^{\mathrm{gate}}_{t}=S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{V}}^{\star})-S^{\star}(a_{\mathrm{pol}})\in[0,\infty]. (19)

The selective procedure gives

ℒtdep\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{dep}} ={Γtgate,jt=0,S⋆​(a𝒱⋆)−S⋆​(a^),jt=1,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\Gamma^{\mathrm{gate}}_{t},&j_{t}=0,\\ S^{\star}(a_{\mathcal{V}}^{\star})-S^{\star}(\widehat{a}),&j_{t}=1,\end{cases} (20)
ℒtdep\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{dep}} ≤Γtcov+Γtrej+ε,jt=1.\displaystyle\leq\Gamma^{\mathrm{cov}}_{t}+\Gamma^{\mathrm{rej}}_{t}+\varepsilon,\qquad j_{t}=1. (21)

The first line is an identity; the bound applies only when jt=1j_{t}=1 and the assumptions of Theorem 2 hold. The jt=0j_{t}=0 branch covers initial gate acceptance, empty-set fallback, and final authorization veto. Its loss Γtgate\Gamma^{\mathrm{gate}}_{t} can be infinite: if Zfeas​(ℋt,apol)=0Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a_{\mathrm{pol}})=0, then S⋆​(apol)=−∞S^{\star}(a_{\mathrm{pol}})=-\infty. Triggering reranking alone therefore does not give a bound on the executed action.

3.3 VICS: Selective Feasible-Future Reranking

A policy can remain confident in a move that has repeatedly failed, even as the observed transition history gives the decoder reason to doubt that another attempt will bring the task any closer to completion. VICS (Viability-Corrected Sampling) acts on this evidence selectively, preserving the policy sample unless the gate invokes reranking and a replacement is authorized. Within this framework, VICS-G supplies the generic ranking, and VICS-S introduces task-grounded rules for selecting among the alternatives. The pre-action interface ℐt=(ot,x,ht,mt)\mathcal{I}_{t}=(o_{t},x,h_{t},m_{t}) includes monitor information mtm_{t}: recent execution outcomes, simulator-provided safety costs, object visibility, and target distance.

VICS-G (Generic VICS).

On intervention, VICS-G ranks admitted candidates by

SG​(a)=log⁡πθ​(a∣ℋt)+λc​ρ^loc​(ℐt,a)+ηv​zG​(ℐt,a).S_{G}(a)=\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})+\lambda_{c}\widehat{\rho}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{I}_{t},a)+\eta_{v}z_{G}(\mathcal{I}_{t},a). (22)

In this practical instantiation, task preference comes from the frozen policy prior, without a separate estimate of the local reward in Equation 13. The omitted β​Rloc\beta R_{\mathrm{loc}} contribution is included in the local score error analyzed in Appendix D.

The local term scores monitored risk; the bounded correction zGz_{G} favors alternatives to recent failure loops through fixed action-type preferences and penalties for repetition and failed or collision-linked retries. All six main settings share score coefficients and weights (Appendix F.1); admission rules are task dependent.

Approximating the future term.

VICS-G uses fixed features of the current monitor and recent execution history as an inexpensive proxy for future viability. The score is not a calibrated estimate of log⁡Z¯feas⋆\log\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star} and does not certify support, so the recovery guarantee remains conditional on the total-score error in Equation 15; Appendix D separates the local and continuation terms.

When the continuation process can be branched, sampled outcomes provide explicit evidence about the futures a candidate leaves open. Corollary 1 gives sufficient conditions under which independent samples from the frozen continuation law preserve the ideal score maximizer. Our simulator-assisted extension, VICS-R, explores this idea using continuations under VICS-G from a reconstructed simulator state (Section 4.4). Its continuation law and selection rule differ from the exact target; Appendix H specifies the estimated quantity and protocol. A learned safe-completion critic offers another possible approximation, which we leave to future work.

VICS-S (Symbolic-support VICS).

Which actions enter the comparison can matter as much as how they are ranked. In its canonical form, VICS-S reflects the support–magnitude distinction: task knowledge constrains eligibility, while the generic score ranks the alternatives that remain. For PickUp and ObjectNav, this yields

ℬtS={a∈ℬt:χ^S​(ℐt,a)=1},aS=arg​maxa∈ℬtS⁡SG​(a).\mathcal{B}_{t}^{S}=\{a\in\mathcal{B}_{t}:\widehat{\chi}_{S}(\mathcal{I}_{t},a)=1\},\qquad a_{S}=\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{S}}S_{G}(a). (23)

Here χ^S=1\widehat{\chi}_{S}=1 indicates eligibility under the task rules, and the maximizer is taken when ℬtS≠∅\mathcal{B}_{t}^{S}\neq\emptyset. These rules provide partial information about support and do not certify viability. The symbolic variants are task-specific diagnostics; Appendix F describes their realization, including the distinct selection rule used for Fetch.

Execution rule.

For VICS-G, the gate invokes reranking when the sample repeats a failed or collision-linked action, fails terminal admission, or has an explicit hard prohibition. An empty surviving set or final authorization veto retains the sample. Algorithm 1 gives the full procedure, including the symbolic terminal boundary.

Comparator and zero-weight ablation.

The RCD selection rule and the zero-weight VICS-G proposal are inspired by SafeDec (Kapoor et al., 2025) and adapted to our evaluation’s policy interface and safety monitors. The baseline uses K=12K=12 in the main and feedback studies, and selects

aRCD\displaystyle a_{\mathrm{RCD}} =arg​maxa∈𝒜RCD⁡SRCD​(a),\displaystyle=\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{RCD}}}S_{\mathrm{RCD}}(a), (24)
a^G,0\displaystyle\widehat{a}_{G,0} =arg​maxa∈ℬt⁡[log⁡πθ​(a∣ℋt)+λc​ρ^loc​(ℐt,a)].\displaystyle=\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})+\lambda_{c}\widehat{\rho}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{I}_{t},a)\right].

Here 𝒜RCD\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{RCD}} and SRCDS_{\mathrm{RCD}} denote the baseline’s candidate set and local-robustness score. The second line applies when reranking is invoked and ℬt≠∅\mathcal{B}_{t}\neq\emptyset; execution still requires replacement authorization. Setting ηv=0\eta_{v}=0 removes only the zGz_{G} correction, retaining VICS-G’s gate, trust region, filters, history-dependent local score, and fallback.

4 Experimental Evaluation

We assess safety gains alongside task completion and episode length. The six task/checkpoint comparisons assess the complete decoder under realistic operating conditions; matched studies then isolate the incremental value of the continuation correction and execution feedback. A separate rollout ablation asks whether looking ahead can further improve the safety–completion trade-off.

4.1 Evaluation protocol

Benchmark and policies.

Safety-CHORES (Zhang et al., 2025) evaluates safety-critical mobile manipulation in procedurally generated indoor environments. We use its PickUp, ObjectNav, and Fetch task families with both task-optimized and safety-aligned SafeVLA checkpoints. All methods use the same episode sets and seeds within each task/checkpoint setting: 160160 PickUp, 200200 ObjectNav, and 172172 Fetch episodes per method. Policy weights remain fixed throughout.

For the generic VICS-G decoder, we use one shared configuration across all six settings, selected using approximately 10%10\% of episodes per task family; the reported results cover the full episode sets. The main comparisons evaluate complete decoders. The zero-weight ablation retains the recovery architecture and isolates the continuation correction, feedback masking isolates the additional execution channel, and Switch after failure tests a simple retry alternative. These matched and supplementary controls clarify how individual components contribute to the overall result.

Methods and measures.

We compare policy sampling (no reranking), RCD, VICS-G, and VICS-S. All reranking methods use K=12K=12 unless otherwise stated; full configurations are reported in Appendix F. We report success (rate and count), mean cumulative cost, violations, and episode length. Appendices I and G give paired feedback and weight analyses. The rollout ablation uses fresh baselines in a modified simulator (Section 4.4; Appendix H). The six-setting results are descriptive; feedback tests are prespecified, while the weight study is exploratory.

4.2 Main results

Lower safety cost across all six settings at near-policy completion.

VICS-G lowers observed mean safety cost by 1.9%1.9\%–57.5%57.5\% and records fewer violations in every setting, spanning both task-optimized and safety-aligned checkpoints. Success stays within 2.52.5 percentage points of policy sampling, and mean episode length remains within 0.820.82 steps. The lower cost thus accompanies sustained task progress.

Task-grounded rules yield complementary gains.

VICS-S reaches its strongest joint gain on base Fetch: success rises by 3.53.5 points, cost falls by 46.0%46.0\%, and violations fall by 41.5%41.5\%. It matches or improves policy success in four settings and lowers cost in five by 10.3%10.3\%–47.3%47.3\%. Safety-aligned Fetch marks the trade-off: highest success (58.7%58.7\%) comes with higher cost and longer episodes. These task-specific profiles complement the consistent observed cost reductions of the generic decoder.

Task progress distinguishes the operating points.

RCD attains lower raw cost, but its success falls by 3.53.5–20.320.3 percentage points and its episodes shorten by 4.44.4–37.537.5 steps relative to policy sampling. Appendix A illustrates these cost–completion trade-offs through navigation recovery and a successful grasp of the requested object.

The continuation correction adds setting-dependent gains.

At ηv=0.10\eta_{v}=0.10, matched sweeps record fewer violations in five of six settings and lower mean cost in four than at zero weight. Success is unchanged on both PickUp checkpoints and Fetch-safe. ObjectNav-base is the adverse case: cost and violations rise, and success falls by 3.003.00 points. This ablation isolates the added zGz_{G} term; history-based recovery remains active at zero weight. Fetch sweeps use all 2020 actions, so they do not decompose the main top-1212 result. Paired intervals and full comparisons appear in Appendix G.

4.3 Execution feedback under imperfect execution

On safety-aligned Fetch, we test whether feedback from the preceding action helps VICS-G adapt to imperfect execution. Using the full evaluation set, we compare policy sampling and VICS-G with and without this feedback. The feedback-aware decoder receives the preceding commanded-versus-realized transition record; masking removes this record while preserving the policy observation interface. We perturb action magnitudes either independently at each step (IID) or by a fixed factor per motion channel throughout the episode (episode-persistent), with ρ=0.1\rho=0.1. Each task is run twice with different perturbations, matched across methods, to reduce dependence on a single noise draw.

Unperturbed runs and the supplementary RCD and Switch after failure baselines were added after the initial results. Their definitions and analyses remain separate from the prespecified tests (Appendix I).

Safety gains extend to imperfect execution.

The feedback-aware decoder reaches 55.67%55.67\% success with 15.9%15.9\% lower observed cost and 16.6%16.6\% fewer violations than policy sampling at virtually identical mean episode length (Table 2). It leads the five methods in pooled success and safe success, with lower cost than policy sampling, Switch after failure, and masked feedback. RCD reaches the lowest cost with 37.79%37.79\% success and shorter episodes.

Feedback meets the success criterion with favorable safety estimates.

Against the same decoder with feedback masked, feedback yields 9.7%9.7\% lower observed cost and a +0.58+0.58-point success difference (95%95\% interval [−1.16,2.33][-1.16,2.33]), meeting the preset 55-point tolerance. The cost interval spans zero, so confirmatory testing stops before the policy comparisons (Table 9). Clean-condition cost estimates favor masking (Table 8); the favorable safety pattern is specific to the tested perturbations.

4.4 Looking ahead to preserve safe completion

The theory motivates a direct test of rollouts: at β=λ=0\beta=\lambda=0, feasible-future mass is the probability of safe completion under the frozen policy (Equation 7). Scaling these estimates to many actions and decision points is costly even in simulation, and their reliability remains tied to the fidelity of the dynamics and contact models (Pinneri et al., 2021; Le Lidec et al., 2024). We therefore study a modest rollout augmentation of VICS-G that tests this criterion under a limited simulation budget.

VICS-R uses at most one early lookahead decision. At an eligible step, it compares the current action with up to two admissible alternatives, samples four continuations per candidate, and executes the candidate with the highest estimated probability of zero-cost completion. It then returns control to VICS-G. These rollouts follow the deployed decoder from a reconstructed simulator state; the ideal-ranking guarantee in Corollary 1 requires the history-conditioned frozen-policy law and its associated scoring assumptions. All methods are rerun in the modified, branchable simulator, separately from Table 1.

On safety-aligned Fetch, VICS-R improves observed safe success over VICS-G from 27.91%27.91\% to 30.23%30.23\%, with task success unchanged at 58.72%58.72\%. Mean cost falls from 3.2333.233 to 3.1163.116 (3.6%3.6\%). These gains illustrate how a limited rollout budget can strengthen VICS-G by adding explicit evidence of safe completion. Full results, branching checks, and the selection protocol appear in Appendix H.

4.5 Limitations

Our evaluation covers three simulated task families, with execution feedback tested under two execution perturbation models at one severity. Broader disturbances and deployment on physical robots remain future work. The decoder relies on heuristic continuation scores, partial symbolic rules, and a selective intervention gate, so its gains may vary across tasks and checkpoints. The theoretical bounds are conditional on score accuracy and candidate coverage. The rollout extension changes the continuation law and adds an intervention opportunity; it neither isolates the additive continuation score nor certifies exact simulator-state restoration.

5 Conclusion

Feasible-future decoding connects safe action selection to the task-completing futures each action leaves open. Its exact target gives this principle a mathematical foundation, and VICS-G turns it into a practical, training-free decoder for frozen VLA policies. Across the evaluated tasks and checkpoints, selective intervention reduces observed safety cost while retaining near-policy completion and sustained task progress. Execution feedback and simulator lookahead extend the approach to richer deployment settings. This offers a path toward safer VLA execution: preserve the policy’s capabilities, intervene selectively, and use continuation evidence to keep safe completion within reach.

AI use statement

We used LLMs for writing and editing assistance, coding assistance, checking the consistency of mathematical derivations, and assisting with the interpretation of experimental results. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final content.

Appendix A Qualitative Episode Comparisons

These episodes illustrate the intended role of VICS-G: local action corrections can preserve progress toward task completion. The navigation case shows recovery from repeated failed moves; the Fetch case shows continued interaction leading to the intended grasp. In both comparisons, VICS-G completes the task at lower cost than policy sampling, while RCD incurs less cost but terminates unsuccessfully. These selected cases complement the aggregate results in Section 4.

A.1 Navigation: recovering from failed retries

This is the main-evaluation episode previewed in Figure 1; the full view below adds the cost trace and the timing of action replacements. It illustrates recovery and task completion, rather than certifying the latent feasible-future mass.

Policy sampling and VICS-G share their first 6868 executed actions before diverging near the region highlighted in Figure 3. Policy sampling keeps retrying failed forward moves, accumulates cost, and eventually terminates without success. VICS-G replaces some of these retries with turns and backward moves, resumes progress, and completes the navigation task. RCD instead ends near the difficult region. The cost trace makes the distinction clear: VICS-G continues after its cost levels off, whereas the low-cost RCD trajectory has already terminated.

A.2 Fetch: completing the intended grasp

This supplementary case uses the modified simulator with a 600600-action budget, separate from the main evaluation and the 200200-action rollout study.

All three methods first reach the same view of a houseplant beside a book (Figure 4). Their subsequent interaction leads to different outcomes. Policy sampling eventually grasps the book and terminates with the wrong object. RCD ends shortly after the shared view, without acquiring an object. VICS-G continues adjusting its approach and arm position, then grasps the requested houseplant. Its safety cost is lower than policy sampling’s and higher than RCD’s. Reading cost alongside the frames explains the trade-off: VICS-G completes the grasp, while RCD’s lower cost accompanies an unfinished task.

Appendix B History-Conditioned Robot Decoding

Let xx be a task instruction and ℋt=(x,o≤t,a<t)\mathcal{H}_{t}=(x,o_{\leq t},a_{<t}) the observable history. A frozen vision-language-action policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, the environment dynamics, and the observation process jointly induce the future-trajectory law p0​(τ∣ℋt)p_{0}(\tau\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}). Let 𝒢x\mathcal{G}_{x} contain trajectories that complete xx within the designated hard safety budget, and let Rx​(τ)R_{x}(\tau) and C⁡(τ)C(\tau) denote total reward and safety cost. We first derive the distribution supported on safe task completion, then examine its finite-candidate approximations.

B.1 Reference trajectory target

Among trajectory distributions that assign probability one to safe task completion, consider

q⋆=arg​minq:q⁡(𝒢x)=1{KL(q(τ)∥p0(τ∣ℋt))−β𝔼q[Rx(τ)]+λ𝔼q[C(τ)]}.q^{\star}=\argmin_{q:\,q(\mathcal{G}_{x})=1}\left\{\mathrm{KL}\!\left(q(\tau)\,\|\,p_{0}(\tau\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\right)-\beta\mathbb{E}_{q}[R_{x}(\tau)]+\lambda\mathbb{E}_{q}[C(\tau)]\right\}. (25)
Proposition 1 (Prior-preserving feasible target).

Assume bounded total reward and cost over the finite horizon and positive prior probability of safe completion. For λ,β≥0\lambda,\beta\geq 0, the unique solution of Equation 25, up to p0p_{0}-null trajectories, is

q⋆​(τ∣ℋt)=p0(τ∣ℋt)𝟏{τ∈𝒢x}eβ​Rx​(τ)−λ​C​(τ)Z⁡(ℋt),q^{\star}(\tau\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})=\frac{p_{0}(\tau\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\mathbf{1}\{\tau\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\}e^{\beta R_{x}(\tau)-\lambda C(\tau)}}{Z(\mathcal{H}_{t})}, (26)

where Z⁡(ℋt)Z(\mathcal{H}_{t}) is the finite, positive normalizing constant.

This is the standard exponential-tilt construction from KL-regularized control and control as inference (Todorov, 2006; Toussaint, 2009; Levine, 2018); it is stated here to make the reference measure and regularity conditions explicit.

Robot model and trajectory law.

The model separates the robot’s latent state from the history available to the policy. We use the partially observable decision process

ℳx=(𝒮,𝒪,𝒜,P,Ω,Rx,C,γ),\mathcal{M}_{x}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A},P,\Omega,R_{x},C,\gamma),

where st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} is latent physical state, ot∼Ω(⋅∣st)o_{t}\sim\Omega(\cdot\mid s_{t}) is the observation, and at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} is an action or action token; γ\gamma is the discount factor. The policy is queried in blocks, so a≡at:t+H−1a\equiv a_{t:t+H-1} induces

st+H∼PH(⋅∣st,a).s_{t+H}\sim P_{H}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a). (27)

Writing the observable history in expanded form,

ℋt=(x,o≤t,a<t),\mathcal{H}_{t}=(x,o_{\leq t},a_{<t}), (28)

the frozen policy πθ(⋅∣ℋt)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}), PP, and Ω\Omega induce the trajectory law p0​(τ∣ℋt)p_{0}(\tau\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}). With

bt​(d​s)=Pr⁡(st∈d​s∣ℋt),b_{t}(ds)=\Pr(s_{t}\in ds\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}),

the candidate-conditioned suffix law is

p0​(ξ∣ℋt,a)=∫p0​(ξ∣s,ℋt,a)​bt​(𝑑s).p_{0}(\xi\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=\int p_{0}(\xi\mid s,\mathcal{H}_{t},a)\,b_{t}(ds). (29)

Here ξ\xi includes the candidate block’s random execution and its subsequent continuation. The integral specifies how latent-state uncertainty enters the reference law; it does not require the deployed decoder to reconstruct a belief state.

Remaining-budget state.

For a cumulative safety budget dd and observed accumulated cost C<tC_{<t}, let dt=d−C<td_{t}=d-C_{<t} denote the budget remaining at history ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}. The same blockwise construction applies to the augmented history ℋ~t=(ℋt,dt)\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{t}=(\mathcal{H}_{t},d_{t}), and a candidate-conditioned realization is feasible only if

Csuf​(ξ)≤dt−Cloc​(ℋ~t,a).C_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi)\leq d_{t}-C_{\mathrm{loc}}(\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{t},a).

Here ClocC_{\mathrm{loc}} is fixed given the augmented history and candidate, while CsufC_{\mathrm{suf}} includes random costs incurred during the block. The realized post-block budget therefore remains inside the continuation expectation. This additive decomposition requires the remaining budget to be part of the decision state.

A test-time decoder receives ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} and a finite set 𝒜K⊆suppπθ(⋅∣ℋt)\mathcal{A}_{K}\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}), and returns D⁡(ℋt,𝒜K)∈𝒜KD(\mathcal{H}_{t},\mathcal{A}_{K})\in\mathcal{A}_{K}.

Unweighted and weighted continuation mass.

Write a future realization as (a,ξ)(a,\xi), with reward and cost decomposed as Rx=Rloc+RsufR_{x}=R_{\mathrm{loc}}+R_{\mathrm{suf}} and C=Cloc+CsufC=C_{\mathrm{loc}}+C_{\mathrm{suf}}. Only terms determined by (ℋt,a)(\mathcal{H}_{t},a) enter the local contributions; stochastic execution costs remain in the suffix. The weighted continuation mass is

Zfeas(ℋt,a)=𝔼ξ∼p0(⋅∣ℋt,a)[𝟏{(a,ξ)∈𝒢x}eβ​Rsuf​(ξ,x)−λ​Csuf​(ξ)].Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim p_{0}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},a)}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{(a,\xi)\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\}e^{\beta R_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi,x)-\lambda C_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi)}\right]. (30)

The corresponding probability of safe completion is

Φ(ℋt,a)=ℙp0[τ∈𝒢x∣ℋt,a].\Phi(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=\mathbb{P}_{p_{0}}[\tau\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},a]. (31)

When β=λ=0\beta=\lambda=0, Zfeas​(ℋt,a)=Φ⁡(ℋt,a)Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=\Phi(\mathcal{H}_{t},a). A finite, strictly positive exponential weight preserves support: Zfeas​(ℋt,a)>0Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)>0 exactly when Φ⁡(ℋt,a)>0\Phi(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)>0. Reward–cost weighting changes the mass of feasible continuations while preserving whether that mass is positive.

Execution feedback.

The continuation mass depends on the transition law, so uncertain execution changes the futures associated with a candidate. The experiment in Appendix I tests whether access to the preceding commanded-versus-realized transition helps the decoder use this information at the next decision.

Scope of the per-decision guarantee.

The finite-candidate bound in Appendix C.3 applies at a fixed history. Extending it to a full trajectory would require control over how approximation errors accumulate: each selected action changes the next history, candidate set, and feasible continuations. Such a result would need uniform error bounds over reachable histories and an argument linking the per-decision bounds across time. We do not assume these stronger conditions.

Sound rejection gives 𝒢t=ℱt\mathcal{G}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{t} and hence Γtrej=0\Gamma^{\mathrm{rej}}_{t}=0. Complete rejection also gives ℛt=∅\mathcal{R}_{t}=\emptyset, so support separation is automatic. With no hard rejection, all viable candidates remain, but the practical score must separate them from the surviving dead ends.

Let apola_{\mathrm{pol}} be the policy sample and jt=1j_{t}=1 indicate that reranking is invoked, its surviving set is nonempty, and replacement is authorized. The executed action is a^\widehat{a} when jt=1j_{t}=1 and apola_{\mathrm{pol}} otherwise. Include apola_{\mathrm{pol}} in 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} whenever it is viable. The bound applies on the jt=1j_{t}=1 branch under the stated assumptions. C.4 Safe-Dead-End Separation

Proposition 2 (Safe-dead-end separation).

There exist two policy-supported candidates with equal likelihood and equal local reward–cost terms such that one has positive feasible-future mass and the other has zero feasible-future mass. Every decoder based only on the shared local quantities is indifferent between them, whereas the ideal blockwise rule excludes the dead end.

Proof.

Consider two candidates aa and bb with equal likelihood and equal local reward and cost. Let aa reach a state from which at least one safe successful suffix has positive probability under the frozen continuation policy, and let bb reach a state from which every policy-supported suffix fails or violates the hard budget. Then Zfeas​(ℋt,a)>0Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)>0 and Zfeas​(ℋt,b)=0Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},b)=0. Every local-information score is equal on the pair. By Equation 37, candidate bb receives log⁡Zfeas​(ℋt,b)=log⁡0=−∞\log Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},b)=\log 0=-\infty, whereas aa has positive feasible-future mass; hence the ideal rule selects aa. ∎

Appendix D Score Error and Rollout Recovery

The generic Viability-Corrected Sampling rule (VICS-G) uses pre-action information ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}, comprising the observable history and available safety-monitor observations. Its score is

SG​(a)=log⁡πθ​(a∣ℋt)+λc​ρ^loc​(ℐt,a)+ηv​zG​(ℐt,a),S_{G}(a)=\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})+\lambda_{c}\widehat{\rho}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{I}_{t},a)+\eta_{v}z_{G}(\mathcal{I}_{t},a), (41)

where ρ^loc\widehat{\rho}_{\mathrm{loc}} is local robustness and zGz_{G} is a continuation correction, with nonnegative weights λc,ηv\lambda_{c},\eta_{v}. Appendix F.1 defines the evaluated scores. Write Z¯feas⋆=Zfeas\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}=Z_{\mathrm{feas}} on viable candidates and set Z¯feas⋆=1\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}=1 otherwise; this neutral convention separates support from positive continuation magnitude.

Sources of score error.

Ranking error comes from both the local robustness term and the continuation correction. For retained viable candidates a,ba,b, suppress common conditioning and define

eloc​(a,b)=\displaystyle e_{\mathrm{loc}}(a,b)={} λc​[ρ^loc​(a)−ρ^loc​(b)]−([β​Rloc​(a)−λ​Cloc​(a)]−[β​Rloc​(b)−λ​Cloc​(b)]),\displaystyle\lambda_{c}\!\left[\widehat{\rho}_{\mathrm{loc}}(a)-\widehat{\rho}_{\mathrm{loc}}(b)\right]-\Bigl([\beta R_{\mathrm{loc}}(a)-\lambda C_{\mathrm{loc}}(a)]-[\beta R_{\mathrm{loc}}(b)-\lambda C_{\mathrm{loc}}(b)]\Bigr), (42)
efut​(a,b)=\displaystyle e_{\mathrm{fut}}(a,b)={} ηv​[zG​(a)−zG​(b)]−[log⁡Z¯feas⋆​(a)−log⁡Z¯feas⋆​(b)].\displaystyle\eta_{v}[z_{G}(a)-z_{G}(b)]-[\log\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}(a)-\log\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}(b)].

Because Zfeas=Z¯feas⋆>0Z_{\mathrm{feas}}=\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{feas}}^{\star}>0 on 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t},

|[SG​(a)−SG​(b)]−[S⋆​(a)−S⋆​(b)]|≤|eloc​(a,b)|+|efut​(a,b)|.\left|[S_{G}(a)-S_{G}(b)]-[S^{\star}(a)-S^{\star}(b)]\right|\leq|e_{\mathrm{loc}}(a,b)|+|e_{\mathrm{fut}}(a,b)|. (43)

Thus local-score mismatch and the scale of ηv​zG\eta_{v}z_{G} enter the same pairwise error ε\varepsilon in Equation 38. The experiments measure task outcomes and compare decoder variants; they do not estimate these latent score errors.

Finite-sample recovery from continuation rollouts.

Feasible-future mass is an expectation under the frozen continuation law, so a branchable model lets us estimate the ideal future term by sampling continuations. For decoding, the key question is whether these estimates preserve the candidate ordering. The next result gives a sufficient rollout budget in terms of the feasible-mass floor and the ideal score margin.

Corollary 1 (Finite-sample rollout recovery).

Let 𝒰t\mathcal{U}_{t} contain NN policy-supported candidates and at least two viable candidates. For each a∈𝒰ta\in\mathcal{U}_{t}, draw nn independent suffixes ξa,i∼p0(⋅∣ℋt,a)\xi_{a,i}\sim p_{0}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},a) and set

Wa,i=𝟏{(a,ξa,i)∈𝒢x}exp(βRsuf(ξa,i,x)−λCsuf(ξa,i)),Z^n(a)=1n∑i=1nWa,i.W_{a,i}=\mathbf{1}\{(a,\xi_{a,i})\in\mathcal{G}_{x}\}\exp\!\left(\beta R_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi_{a,i},x)-\lambda C_{\mathrm{suf}}(\xi_{a,i})\right),\qquad\widehat{Z}_{n}(a)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}W_{a,i}.

Assume 0≤Wa,i≤M0\leq W_{a,i}\leq M almost surely and Zfeas​(ℋt,a)≥zmin>0Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)\geq z_{\min}>0 for every viable candidate. Define

B⁡(a)=log⁡πθ​(a∣ℋt)+β​Rloc​(ℋt,a)−λ​Cloc​(ℋt,a),B(a)=\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})+\beta R_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)-\lambda C_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a),

and let a⋆a^{\star} be the unique maximizer of B⁡(a)+log⁡Zfeas​(ℋt,a)B(a)+\log Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a) over viable actions, with margin Δ>0\Delta>0. For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), let ρΔ=1−e−Δ/4\rho_{\Delta}=1-e^{-\Delta/4}. If

n≥M22​zmin2​ρΔ2​log⁡2​Nδ,n\geq\frac{M^{2}}{2z_{\min}^{2}\rho_{\Delta}^{2}}\log\frac{2N}{\delta}, (44)

then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

arg​maxa∈𝒰t⁡{B⁡(a)+log⁡Z^n​(a)}=a⋆,\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{U}_{t}}\{B(a)+\log\widehat{Z}_{n}(a)\}=a^{\star},

with log⁡0=−∞\log 0=-\infty. Every zero-support candidate satisfies Z^n​(a)=0\widehat{Z}_{n}(a)=0 almost surely.

Proof.

Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound give, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

|Z^n​(a)−Zfeas​(ℋt,a)|≤ρΔ​zmin∀a∈𝒰t.|\widehat{Z}_{n}(a)-Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)|\leq\rho_{\Delta}z_{\min}\qquad\forall a\in\mathcal{U}_{t}.

For every viable aa, this is a relative error of at most ρΔ\rho_{\Delta}, so

e−Δ/4≤Z^n​(a)Zfeas​(ℋt,a)≤eΔ/4.e^{-\Delta/4}\leq\frac{\widehat{Z}_{n}(a)}{Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)}\leq e^{\Delta/4}.

Each log mass is therefore accurate within Δ/4\Delta/4, and every pairwise margin changes by at most Δ/2\Delta/2; the unique maximizer is preserved. If Zfeas​(ℋt,a)=0Z_{\mathrm{feas}}(\mathcal{H}_{t},a)=0, nonnegativity and zero expectation imply Wa,i=0W_{a,i}=0 almost surely. ∎

For small Δ\Delta, Equation 44 scales as O⁡(M2​zmin−2​Δ−2​log⁡(N/δ))O(M^{2}z_{\min}^{-2}\Delta^{-2}\log(N/\delta)): near ties and rare safe completions demand more rollouts, while a clear winner can be resolved with a modest budget. Here NN counts the candidates actually evaluated, including any retained policy sample, so retaining the sample beside the KK highest-likelihood actions gives N≤K+1N\leq K+1. The result formalizes how the number of continuation samples controls whether the estimated ranking preserves the winner.

Appendix E Exact Finite-Model Examples

Finite two-stage models make the roles of local safety, feasible support, and continuation magnitude explicit. The specified probabilities and weights are rational, so the examples can be evaluated exactly. The weighted examples use β=λ=log⁡2\beta=\lambda=\log 2.

Local safety, support, and magnitude.

Consider the four-action model illustrated in Figure 2:

𝒜={aU,aD,aL,aH},π⁡(aU,aD,aL,aH)=127​(16,8,2,1).\mathcal{A}=\{a_{U},a_{D},a_{L},a_{H}\},\qquad\pi(a_{U},a_{D},a_{L},a_{H})=\frac{1}{27}(16,8,2,1).

Let m=(0,1,1,1)m=(0,1,1,1) be the local-admissibility indicator and χF=(0,0,1,1)\chi_{F}=(0,0,1,1) the true feasible support. Action aUa_{U} violates the local condition immediately; aDa_{D} has a locally admissible prefix but no safe successful suffix. For the supported actions, let

Z¯F​(aL)=14,Z¯F​(aH)=1.\overline{Z}_{F}(a_{L})=\frac{1}{4},\qquad\overline{Z}_{F}(a_{H})=1.

This corresponds to a unit-weight safe-success suffix occurring with probability 1/41/4 or 11, respectively. Thus

27​π​(a)​χF​(a)​Z¯F​(a)=(0,0,12,1),27\,\pi(a)\chi_{F}(a)\overline{Z}_{F}(a)=\left(0,0,\frac{1}{2},1\right),

and normalization gives

qF⋆=(0,0,1/3,2/3).q_{F}^{\star}=(0,0,1/3,2/3).

The policy MAP action is aUa_{U}; local filtering alone selects aDa_{D}; exact support with flat magnitude selects aLa_{L}; and exact support with exact magnitude selects aHa_{H}. Local admissibility removes 16/2716/27 prior mass on aUa_{U}; the dead end aDa_{D} carries 8/118/11 of the locally admitted mass. Magnitude reverses the feasible odds q⁡(aH)/q⁡(aL)q(a_{H})/q(a_{L}) from 1/21/2 to 22. In base-two log units, aHa_{H} exceeds aLa_{L} by exactly one bit. The construction witnesses the distinct roles of immediate safety, feasible support, and within-support magnitude under an ideal rule that evaluates every factor. Under selective intervention, accepting aDa_{D} at the initial gate bypasses the remaining factors. Omitting aHa_{H} is proposal/admission coverage error; rejecting a viable action is false-rejection loss; and selecting aLa_{L} while aHa_{H} is retained is total-score ranking error.

Why local information cannot solve both worlds.

Consider two actions and two equally weighted worlds with identical policy likelihoods and local reward–cost terms. In the first world, only the first action admits safe completion, with probability one; in the second, only the second action does. Any decoder restricted to the shared local quantities uses the same action distribution in both worlds and has mean safe-completion probability 1/21/2. The exact feasible-future rule selects the supported action in each world and succeeds in both. Continuation-dependent information is therefore necessary for uniform success on this pair.

Magnitude when safe completion is certain.

Table 3 uses three actions (bD,bL,bH)(b_{D},b_{L},b_{H}) with equal priors and one deterministic suffix per action. Their safe-success indicators are (0,1,1)(0,1,1), suffix rewards are (0,0,2)(0,0,2), and suffix costs are zero. Thus both supported actions succeed surely, unlike aLa_{L} in the four-action witness. For every action we enumerate

ZF​(a)=∑ξp⁡(ξ∣a)​𝟏​{ξ​ is safe and successful}​2R⁡(ξ)​2−C⁡(ξ),Z_{F}(a)=\sum_{\xi}p(\xi\mid a)\mathbf{1}\{\xi\text{ is safe and successful}\}2^{R(\xi)}2^{-C(\xi)}, (45)

and verify exactly that

ZF​(a)=χF​(a)​Z¯F​(a),Z_{F}(a)=\chi_{F}(a)\,\overline{Z}_{F}(a),

using the neutral convention Z¯F​(a)=1\overline{Z}_{F}(a)=1 when χF​(a)=0\chi_{F}(a)=0. We then hold the local base-two scores fixed at (3,1,0)(3,1,0) and set ηv=1\eta_{v}=1. The hard masses are (0,1,4)(0,1,4) and the within-support log magnitudes are (0,0,2)(0,0,2), including the neutral zero-support convention. The four combinations of support rejection and magnitude scoring produce the table’s four decisions. Regret is the ideal score of the exact supported optimum minus the selected action’s ideal score; it is +∞+\infty for bDb_{D}, whose ideal score is −∞-\infty. Exact support is enough to avoid the dead end; exact magnitude is additionally required to choose the higher-valued feasible continuation.

Finite candidates and partial support.

Enumerating candidate subsets separates the three sources of loss in Appendix C.3: missing viable proposals, rejecting viable candidates, and misranking the viable survivors. Sound rejection makes the false-rejection term zero, complete rejection removes all unresolved dead ends, and a no-rejection rule still requires the practical score to rank a viable action above every unresolved dead end. Under a declared pairwise total-score error bound ε\varepsilon, the enumerated within-set regret is at most ε\varepsilon.

These finite models make the support, magnitude, coverage, rejection, and ranking effects exact; the deployed decoder approximates the corresponding quantities through the rules specified in Appendix F.

Appendix F Decoding Rules and Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate frozen, task-optimized (base) and safety-aligned (safe) SafeVLA policies on Safety-CHORES (Zhang et al., 2025): 160160 PickUp, 200200 ObjectNav, and 172172 Fetch episodes per method and checkpoint. Methods share episode sets and randomization within each setting. The generic rule (VICS-G) shares its coefficients across all six settings; the symbolic variant (VICS-S) adds task-specific eligibility rules. These coefficients were selected using approximately 10%10\% of episodes per task family; reported results use the full sets. These main comparisons use information available before execution, without simulating candidate futures.

We report task success, cumulative safety cost, violation count, and episode length jointly. Safe success requires task completion with zero violations. Algorithm 1 gives the generic rule and the PickUp/ObjectNav symbolic variants; Fetch uses the separate symbolic selection rule described below.

F.1 Generic Score and Execution Rule

Inputs and shared settings.

The policy receives RGB observations, the instruction, and history. The safety monitor also observes executed actions, action failures, collisions, simulator-provided costs, visible-object identities, and target visibility and distance. The evaluation therefore assumes access to these monitoring signals in addition to images. Visibility and distance affect admission and progress checks, but do not enter zGz_{G}. Unavailable costs, counts, and history contribute zero; unobserved events are treated as absent. All six settings use sampling temperature one and (λc,ηv)=(1,.1)(\lambda_{c},\eta_{v})=(1,.1) in Equation 41.

Table 4 supplies the action coefficients. Because both matching criteria contribute, 0≤nt≤100\leq n_{t}\leq 10 and −12.85≤zG≤.35-12.85\leq z_{G}\leq.35. Scores are not standardized, normalized, or clipped; the displayed correction omits only a candidate-independent offset.

Symbolic variants.

PickUp and ObjectNav retain the generic candidates and score. Define χ^S​(ℐt,a)=0\widehat{\chi}_{S}(\mathcal{I}_{t},a)=0 when a symbolic rule rejects premature pickup, invalid release, or premature termination, and 11 otherwise. The symbolic variant ranks only ℬtS={a∈ℬt:χ^S​(ℐt,a)=1}\mathcal{B}_{t}^{S}=\{a\in\mathcal{B}_{t}:\widehat{\chi}_{S}(\mathcal{I}_{t},a)=1\}. These symbolic variants are task-specific diagnostics; their partial rules do not certify complete viability.

Gate and trust-region choices limit when a correction can affect the executed action, as discussed in Appendix C.3. The Robustness Constrained Decoding baseline (RCD) is inspired by SafeDec (Kapoor et al., 2025) and uses the same policy and safety-monitor observations, with K=12K=12 in the benchmark and feedback studies.
